offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (first, no aggravators); 1st Degree Misdemeanor (BAC .15+ or minor present); 3rd Degree Felony (third within 10 years or fourth+)
penalty_max: 6 months (first); 9 months (BAC .15+/minor, first); 5 years (third within 10 yrs or fourth+)
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a vehicle
While driving, defendant was under the influence of alcoholic beverages, chemical substances, or controlled substances
Influence impaired defendant's normal faculties, OR defendant had a BAC of .08 or higher
mandatory_minimum: 8 hours imprisonment or community service (first offense); 10 days imprisonment if BAC .15+ or minor present
enhancements: Third conviction within 10 years (3rd degree felony)
Fourth or subsequent conviction (3rd degree felony)
Serious bodily injury (3rd degree felony under § 316.193(3)(c)2)
Death resulting (DUI manslaughter — 2nd degree felony under § 316.193(3)(c)3)
notes: Implied consent statute § 316.1932. Administrative license suspension separate from criminal penalties. Ignition interlock required for repeat offenses and first-offense BAC .15+.

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence — First Offense
offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a vehicle
While driving, defendant was under the influence of alcohol or controlled substances
Normal faculties impaired OR BAC .08 or higher
No prior DUI convictions
mandatory_minimum: Not less than 8 hours imprisonment or community service; 50 hours community service
notes: Probation up to 1 year. Vehicle impoundment 10 days. 50 hours community service required. First offense is 2nd degree misdemeanor in FL absent aggravating factors.

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence — Repeat Offense
offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor (second); 3rd Degree Felony (third within 10 years or fourth+)
penalty_max: 9 months (second); 5 years (third within 10 years or fourth+)
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a vehicle
While driving, defendant was under the influence
Normal faculties impaired OR BAC .08 or higher
One or more prior DUI convictions
mandatory_minimum: 10 days (second offense); 30 days (third within 10 years)
enhancements: Third conviction within 10 years (3rd degree felony mandatory)
Fourth conviction regardless of time (3rd degree felony)
notes: Mandatory ignition interlock 1 year on second offense; 2 years if BAC .15+. Permanent license revocation possible for fourth or subsequent.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (first offense); escalates same as alcohol DUI
penalty_max: 6 months (first); same escalation as alcohol DUI on subsequent offenses
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a vehicle
While driving, defendant was under the influence of a chemical substance listed in § 877.111 or a controlled substance under Chapter 893
Influence impaired defendant's normal faculties
enhancements: Prescription drugs taken outside prescribed manner
notes: Florida has no per se drug impairment limit. Prosecution must prove impairment of normal faculties. Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) testimony commonly used. DREC evaluation results admissible.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (no injury/damage); 1st Degree Misdemeanor (with property damage/personal injury)
penalty_max: 90 days (first, no injury); 6 months (second+ or with damage); 5 years (serious bodily injury — 3rd degree felony)
elements: Defendant drove a vehicle in Florida
Defendant drove with willful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property
enhancements: Property damage or personal injury (1st degree misdemeanor)
Second or subsequent conviction ($1,000 minimum fine)
notes: Willful and wanton disregard is a higher standard than mere negligence. Commonly charged alongside or as lesser-included of DUI. Racing on public roads is a separate offense under § 316.191.

statute_title: Leaving the Scene of a Crash
offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (property damage only); 3rd Degree Felony (injury); 2nd Degree Felony (serious bodily injury); 1st Degree Felony (death)
penalty_max: 60 days (property); 5 years (injury); 15 years (serious bodily injury); 30 years (death)
elements: Defendant was the driver of a vehicle involved in a crash
The crash resulted in property damage, injury, or death
Defendant knew or reasonably should have known of the crash
Defendant willfully failed to stop and remain at the scene or provide required information
notes: § 316.027 governs crashes with injury/death; § 316.061 governs property-only crashes. Mandatory 4-year minimum for death with failure to stop under § 316.027(2)(c).

offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony; 1st Degree Felony (failure to stop and render aid)
penalty_max: 15 years (2nd degree); 30 years (with failure to stop)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
The operation caused the death of a human being or viable fetus
Operation was reckless — showing conscious disregard for the safety of others
enhancements: Failure to stop and render aid (upgrades to 1st degree felony)
notes: Distinguished from DUI manslaughter (§ 316.193(3)) — vehicular homicide does not require alcohol/drug impairment as a primary element. Both can be charged for the same incident.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony; 1st Degree Felony (leaving scene)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle while under the influence
Operation caused the death of a human being or viable unborn child
mandatory_minimum: 4 years (§ 775.082); permanent driver license revocation
notes: Level 8 offense under Florida's Criminal Punishment Code — state prison presumptive. Mandatory 4-year minimum cannot be suspended. Permanent revocation of driver's license.

statute_title: Driving While License Suspended, Revoked, or Cancelled
offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (first); 1st Degree Misdemeanor (second); 3rd Degree Felony (HTO or third+)
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle on a public road or highway
Defendant's license or driving privilege was suspended, revoked, or cancelled
Defendant had knowledge of the suspension (or constructive notice via mail)
enhancements: Habitual Traffic Offender (HTO) designation — 3rd degree felony
notes: HTO under § 322.264 requires 3+ major violations within 5 years. Knowledge established by proof DMV sent suspension notice. Civil citation available for some violations.

statute_title: Fleeing or Attempting to Elude a Law Enforcement Officer
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (basic); 2nd Degree Felony (high speed/reckless); 1st Degree Felony (serious bodily injury or death)
elements: Defendant was the operator of a motor vehicle
A law enforcement officer in an authorized patrol vehicle with visible emergency lights and siren activated ordered defendant to stop
Defendant willfully fled or attempted to elude the officer
mandatory_minimum: 3 years (§ 316.1935(4) — high-speed fleeing causing serious injury or death)
enhancements: High speed or reckless driving (2nd degree felony)
Serious bodily injury resulting (2nd degree felony)
notes: Both siren and lights must be activated. Mandatory 3-year minimum for high-speed fleeing causing serious injury. License revocation mandatory.

statute_title: Possession of Open Container of Alcoholic Beverage in Vehicle
offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant was the operator or passenger of a vehicle on a public highway
A container of alcoholic beverage with broken seal, missing cap, or partially removed contents was in the passenger area
Defendant possessed the open container
notes: Trunk, locked glove box, or behind last upright rear seat in vehicles without trunks are exceptions. Civil infraction option for passengers in some circumstances.

statute_title: Implied Consent — Refusal to Submit to Test
offense_class: Civil infraction (first); 1st Degree Misdemeanor (second or subsequent refusal)
elements: Defendant was lawfully arrested for DUI
Officer requested defendant submit to breath, blood, or urine test
Defendant was informed of consequences of refusal
Defendant refused to submit
enhancements: Second or subsequent refusal (1st degree misdemeanor criminal charge)
notes: First refusal: 12-month administrative license suspension. Second refusal: 18-month administrative suspension PLUS 1st degree misdemeanor. Refusal admissible as evidence of consciousness of guilt.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor (Schedule III-IV small amount); 3rd Degree Felony (Schedule I-II)
elements: Defendant knew of the presence of the substance
Defendant had actual or constructive possession
The substance was a controlled substance under Chapter 893
enhancements: Within 1,000 feet of school, park, or other protected location (§ 893.13(1)(c)) — 1st degree felony
notes: Florida eliminated knowledge-of-illicit-nature element (§ 893.101). Knowledge of presence sufficient. Drug Court available for eligible defendants.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor (20 grams or less); 3rd Degree Felony (more than 20 grams)
elements: Defendant knew of the presence of the cannabis
Defendant had actual or constructive possession
Substance was cannabis as defined in § 893.02
notes: Medical marijuana defense available under Art. X, § 29 and § 381.986 for licensed holders. Recreational marijuana remained illegal (Amendment 3 failed Nov 2024). Many counties have civil citation ordinances for small amounts.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant knew of the presence of cocaine
Defendant had actual or constructive possession
Substance was cocaine — Schedule II under § 893.03
mandatory_minimum: 3 years (if 28 grams — trafficking threshold under § 893.135)
enhancements: Within 1,000 feet of school (2nd degree felony)
notes: Cocaine is Schedule II. Simple possession under 28g is 3rd degree felony. Lab confirmation required. Chain of custody is a critical defense issue.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant knew of the presence of methamphetamine
Defendant had actual or constructive possession
Substance was methamphetamine — Schedule II
mandatory_minimum: 3 years (14 grams trafficking threshold under § 893.135(1)(d))
notes: Meth trafficking thresholds lower than cocaine. Prior drug conviction can trigger habitual offender sentencing.

statute_title: Possession of Heroin, Fentanyl, or Opioids
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant knew of the presence of the opioid substance
Defendant had actual or constructive possession
Substance was a Schedule I or II opioid (heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone, etc.)
mandatory_minimum: 3 years (4 grams fentanyl/heroin trafficking under § 893.135)
enhancements: Fentanyl causing death (1st degree murder per § 782.04(1)(a)2.z — 2023 law)
notes: 2023 law: delivering fentanyl that causes death can be charged as 1st degree murder. Fentanyl and fentanyl analogs share the 4-gram trafficking threshold. Heroin threshold is also 4 grams.

statute_title: Possession of Prescription Drug Without Valid Prescription
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant possessed a prescription drug
Defendant did not have a valid prescription from a licensed practitioner
OR Defendant obtained the prescription by fraud, misrepresentation, or deception
enhancements: Doctor shopping (multiple prescriptions from different practitioners)
notes: Valid prescription is an affirmative defense. Pill bottle with someone else's name does not establish a valid prescription for the defendant.

offense_class: 1st Degree Felony
penalty_min: 3 years (minimum varies by substance and amount)
elements: Defendant knowingly sold, purchased, manufactured, delivered, or brought into Florida, or was in actual or constructive possession of a controlled substance
The quantity met or exceeded the trafficking threshold for that substance
mandatory_minimum: 3 years (cocaine 28g, heroin/fentanyl 4g, meth 14g, cannabis 25 lbs); escalates to 7, 15, 25 years, or life based on quantity
enhancements: Highest quantity tier (capital trafficking — life or 25-year minimum)
Substantial assistance cooperation (§ 893.135(4)) — only way to mitigate mandatory minimum
notes: Mandatory minimums cannot be suspended, deferred, or withheld. Knowledge of illicit nature is NOT an element per § 893.101. Substantial assistance is the primary mitigation route.

statute_title: Sale, Manufacture, or Delivery of Controlled Substance
offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony (Schedule I-II); 3rd Degree Felony (Schedule III-IV)
elements: Defendant sold, manufactured, or delivered a controlled substance
OR Defendant possessed a controlled substance with intent to sell, manufacture, or deliver
Substance was a controlled substance under Chapter 893
enhancements: Within 1,000 feet of school, park, or playground (1st degree felony)
Within 1,000 feet of place of worship (1st degree felony)
notes: Location-enhanced charges carry significantly higher penalties. Constructive possession plus indicia (scales, bags, cash, messages) supports intent charge.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony (Schedule I-II); 3rd Degree Felony (Schedule III-IV)
elements: Defendant manufactured a controlled substance
Substance was a controlled substance under Chapter 893
Defendant acted knowingly
notes: Manufacturing includes production, preparation, propagation, compounding, or processing. Marijuana cultivation included. Meth lab contamination may implicate additional environmental liability.

statute_title: Use or Possession of Drug Paraphernalia
offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant used or possessed with intent to use drug paraphernalia
Paraphernalia was used or intended to be used in connection with a controlled substance
Defendant acted knowingly
notes: Paraphernalia defined broadly in § 893.145 — pipes, syringes, rolling papers, scales. Intent inferred from proximity to drugs, residue, and statements.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant uttered, published, or passed a forged prescription
Defendant knew the prescription was forged
Defendant acted with intent to injure or defraud
notes: Also prosecuted under § 893.13(7)(a) for obtaining controlled substance by fraud. Both charges often filed simultaneously. Pharmacy surveillance footage commonly used.

statute_title: Possession with Intent to Sell or Deliver
offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony (Schedule I-II); 3rd Degree Felony (Schedule III-V)
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
Defendant possessed with specific intent to sell or deliver
Substance was a controlled substance under Chapter 893
notes: Intent proven circumstantially through quantity, packaging, scales, cash, and text messages. Actual sale need not be proven.

offense_class: Capital Felony; Life Felony
penalty_min: Life without parole (if death penalty not sought)
elements: Defendant unlawfully killed a human being
The killing was premeditated (prior deliberation and reflection), OR
The killing occurred during perpetration or attempted perpetration of an enumerated felony (felony murder)
mandatory_minimum: Life without possibility of parole
notes: Post-Hurst v. Florida (2016) — jury must unanimously recommend death. Felony murder predicate felonies listed in § 782.04(1)(a)2. Fentanyl-induced death added as predicate 2023.

offense_class: 1st Degree Felony (Punishable by Life)
elements: Defendant unlawfully killed a human being
The killing was by an act imminently dangerous to another evincing a depraved mind
Defendant had no premeditated design to cause death
mandatory_minimum: 16.75 years (Criminal Punishment Code Level 10 scoresheet)
notes: Depraved mind murder requires conduct that was extremely dangerous and showed no regard for human life. Less culpable mental state than 1st degree but often charged together as alternative counts.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant killed a human being
Killing was the result of culpable negligence, OR
Killing occurred in sudden heat of passion resulting from adequate provocation
notes: Aggravated manslaughter provisions in § 782.07(2)-(4) carry 30-year maximum. Florida treats voluntary and involuntary manslaughter under same statute.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant killed a human being
Death resulted from defendant's culpable negligence
Culpable negligence is gross and flagrant, showing reckless disregard for human life
enhancements: Victim under 18 (aggravated manslaughter of a child — 1st degree felony)
notes: Culpable negligence standard is higher than civil negligence — more than simple carelessness. Child abuse resulting in death typically charged as aggravated manslaughter of a child.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant intentionally and unlawfully threatened by word or act to do violence to the victim
Defendant appeared to have the ability to carry out the threat
The act created a well-founded fear in the victim that violence was imminent
The assault was made with a deadly weapon without intent to kill, OR with intent to commit a felony
mandatory_minimum: 3 years (10-20-Life if firearm carried); 20 years (firearm discharged)
enhancements: Victim is law enforcement (2nd degree felony)
notes: Assault in Florida requires NO physical contact — it is the threat plus reasonable fear. Battery (§ 784.03) requires actual contact.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant intentionally and unlawfully threatened by word or act to do violence to the victim
Defendant appeared to have the ability to carry out the threat
The act created a well-founded fear in the victim that violence was imminent
enhancements: Use of weapon (elevates to aggravated assault)
notes: Simple assault requires no physical contact — purely threat-based. Often filed with disorderly conduct.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant actually and intentionally touched or struck the victim against the victim's will
OR Defendant intentionally caused bodily harm to the victim
enhancements: Prior battery conviction (felony battery — 3rd degree felony)
Victim is law enforcement, firefighter, healthcare worker (felony battery)
notes: Battery requires actual physical contact; assault does not. Domestic battery (§ 741.028) requires mandatory arrest. Prior battery conviction raises to 3rd degree felony.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant intentionally touched or struck the victim
Defendant intentionally or knowingly caused great bodily harm, permanent disability, or permanent disfigurement
OR Defendant used a deadly weapon during the battery
mandatory_minimum: 10 years (§ 775.087 10-20-Life if firearm used)
enhancements: Victim is law enforcement (1st degree felony)
Victim elderly or disabled (1st degree felony — § 784.08)
notes: Great bodily harm is a higher standard than bodily harm. Aggravated battery on pregnant woman is 1st degree felony under § 784.045(1)(b).

offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony (no weapon); 1st Degree Felony (weapon); Life Felony (firearm or deadly weapon)
penalty_max: 15 years (no weapon); 30 years (with weapon); Life (firearm/deadly weapon)
elements: Defendant took money or other property from the victim or victim's custody
Defendant used force, violence, assault, or putting in fear
Defendant intended to permanently or temporarily deprive the victim of the property
mandatory_minimum: 10 years (10-20-Life if firearm carried)
notes: Home invasion robbery (§ 812.135) is a 1st degree felony with potential life sentence. Carjacking (§ 812.133) is a separate charge.

statute_title: Robbery with a Firearm or Deadly Weapon
offense_class: Life Felony
elements: Defendant took money or other property from the victim
Defendant used force, violence, assault, or putting in fear
Defendant carried a firearm or other deadly weapon during the robbery
mandatory_minimum: 10 years (§ 775.087); 20 years if firearm discharged; 25 years if death or serious bodily injury
enhancements: Death or serious bodily injury (25-year mandatory minimum)
notes: Life felony — maximum life imprisonment. 10-20-Life mandatory minimums cannot be suspended. Firearm need not be loaded or functional for enhancement to apply.

offense_class: 1st Degree Felony (Punishable by Life)
elements: Defendant forcibly, secretly, or by threat confined, abducted, imprisoned, or restrained the victim against his or her will
Defendant did so without lawful authority
Defendant intended to: hold for ransom, use as shield/hostage, commit or facilitate a felony, inflict bodily harm, terrorize, or interfere with government functions
mandatory_minimum: Life if victim under 13 and defendant also convicted of sexual battery
enhancements: Victim under 13 (life felony; capital if sexual battery also charged)
notes: False imprisonment (§ 787.02) is the lesser offense without the felony-intent requirement. Movement must be more than incidental to separate kidnapping from false imprisonment.

offense_class: 1st Degree Felony (occupied structure or dwelling); 2nd Degree Felony (unoccupied structure)
elements: Defendant willfully and unlawfully, or while committing a felony, by fire or explosion
Damaged or caused to be damaged any dwelling, structure, or vehicle
With intent or while the damage was intentional
notes: § 806.01(1) — 1st degree felony for occupied structure or any dwelling. § 806.01(2) — 2nd degree felony for unoccupied structure.

statute_title: Attempted First or Second Degree Murder
offense_class: 1st Degree Felony (attempt 1st degree); Life Felony (with firearm)
elements: Defendant attempted to commit first or second degree murder
Defendant had premeditated intent to kill (for attempted 1st degree)
Defendant committed an overt act toward commission of the murder
mandatory_minimum: 10 years (10-20-Life if firearm used)
notes: Attempt statute § 777.04. Attempted 2nd degree charged when premeditation absent. Attempted murder of law enforcement carries enhanced penalties.

statute_title: Aggravated Assault with a Deadly Weapon
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant intentionally threatened to do violence to the victim
Defendant appeared to have the ability to carry out the threat
Threat created well-founded fear in the victim
Defendant used a deadly weapon without intent to kill
mandatory_minimum: 3 years minimum (firearm carried); 20 years (firearm discharged)
enhancements: Victim is law enforcement (2nd degree felony)
notes: No actual contact required — assault is threat-based in Florida. Deadly weapon includes knife, bat, vehicle, or any object used to threaten death or great bodily harm.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (under $100); 1st Degree Misdemeanor ($100-$749); 3rd Degree Felony ($750-$19,999); 2nd Degree Felony ($20,000-$99,999); 1st Degree Felony ($100,000+)
elements: Defendant knowingly obtained or used, or endeavored to obtain or use, the property of another
Defendant intended to temporarily or permanently deprive the owner of a right to the property or a benefit from it
OR Defendant appropriated the property to his or her own use or to a person not entitled to the use
enhancements: Emergency equipment (1st degree felony regardless of value)
Grand theft of law enforcement equipment
notes: Florida raised felony threshold from $300 to $750 in 2019. Second petit theft conviction = 3rd degree felony. Restitution available. Civil demand allowed for shoplifting under § 772.11.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony ($750-$19,999); 2nd Degree Felony ($20,000-$99,999); 1st Degree Felony ($100,000+)
elements: Defendant knowingly obtained or used property of another
With intent to deprive the owner of the property
Value of property was $750 or more
enhancements: Theft from elderly (mandatory restitution + enhanced penalties)
Emergency equipment (1st degree felony regardless of value)
notes: Special categories regardless of value: firearm, law enforcement badge, stop sign, will, vehicle with person inside. Cargo theft under § 812.019.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (under $100); 1st Degree Misdemeanor ($100-$749)
elements: Defendant knowingly obtained or used property of another
With intent to deprive the owner
Value of property was under $750
enhancements: Prior theft conviction escalates charge level
Two prior petit theft convictions = 3rd degree felony
notes: Third petit theft offense becomes 3rd degree felony. Civil demand letters from merchants allowed under § 772.11.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (under $100); 1st Degree Misdemeanor ($100-$749); 3rd Degree Felony ($750+ or prior conviction)
elements: Defendant took possession of or carried away merchandise
OR Defendant altered/removed a price tag, transferred merchandise, or removed a shopping cart
Defendant intended to deprive the merchant of possession or full retail value
enhancements: Use of booster bag or demagnetizing device
notes: Merchant detention privilege under § 812.015(3). Organized retail theft ring (3+ people, multiple stores) is 2nd degree felony.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (unoccupied structure/conveyance); 2nd Degree Felony (occupied structure or dwelling); 1st Degree Felony (armed or assault/battery during)
elements: Defendant entered a dwelling, structure, or conveyance
At the time of entering, defendant had intent to commit an offense therein
AND defendant entered without permission OR remained after permission was withdrawn
enhancements: Occupied at time of entry (2nd degree felony minimum)
Assault or battery during (1st degree felony — life eligible)
notes: Burglary in Florida does not require nighttime or breaking — any unlawful entry with criminal intent. Remaining concealed in structure also qualifies.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony (unoccupied); 1st Degree Felony (occupied or assault/battery inside)
elements: Defendant entered or remained in a dwelling
Entry was without permission or consent
Defendant intended to commit an offense inside the dwelling
enhancements: Occupied at time of entry (1st degree felony)
notes: Dwelling means any building actually used as a place of abode. Attached garage and curtilage qualify.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (unoccupied); 2nd Degree Felony (occupied or assault/battery)
elements: Defendant entered or remained in a structure (not a dwelling)
Without permission or consent
Defendant intended to commit an offense inside
enhancements: Structure occupied at time of entry (2nd degree felony)
notes: Structure means any building that is not a dwelling (stores, warehouses, schools). Burglary of a conveyance (car) — separate 3rd degree felony.

statute_title: Grand Theft of a Motor Vehicle
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant knowingly obtained or used a motor vehicle belonging to another
Defendant intended to permanently or temporarily deprive the owner
The vehicle was a motor vehicle (all qualify — no value threshold)
enhancements: Carjacking — force or violence (§ 812.133 — life felony)
notes: Motor vehicle theft is automatically grand theft (3rd degree felony) regardless of value. Carjacking (§ 812.133) requires force or violence — 1st degree felony (life eligible with firearm).

offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony (trafficking); 3rd Degree Felony (dealing)
elements: Defendant trafficked in, or endeavored to traffic in, property that defendant knew or should have known was stolen
OR Defendant received, retained, concealed, or withheld from the true owner stolen property
enhancements: Organizer or supervisor of trafficking ring (1st degree felony)
notes: § 812.025 prohibits charging both theft and dealing in stolen property from the same transaction. 'Should have known' standard allows circumstantial evidence of knowledge.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (under $200); 1st Degree Misdemeanor ($200-$999); 3rd Degree Felony ($1,000+)
elements: Defendant willfully and maliciously injured or damaged real or personal property belonging to another
Defendant had no right to damage the property
enhancements: Damage to utility or communications equipment
notes: Restitution is mandatory. Value is replacement or repair cost.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (without warning); 1st Degree Misdemeanor (after warning); 3rd Degree Felony (with weapon)
elements: Defendant willfully entered or remained in a structure or conveyance
Defendant was not authorized, licensed, or invited
OR Defendant remained after permission was withdrawn
enhancements: Armed with dangerous weapon (3rd degree felony)
School grounds during school hours (3rd degree felony)
notes: Trespass in a structure (§ 810.08) vs. trespass on property (§ 810.09) are separate charges. School trespass during hours is automatic 3rd degree felony.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (under $200); 1st Degree Misdemeanor ($200-$999); 3rd Degree Felony ($1,000+)
elements: Defendant willfully and maliciously injured or damaged real or personal property belonging to another
Defendant had no legal right to damage the property
enhancements: Damage to utility or communications equipment
notes: Florida uses 'criminal mischief' not 'vandalism.' Restitution mandatory. Graffiti specifically addressed in § 806.13(3).

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor minimum (domestic battery); escalates with underlying charge
penalty_min: 5 days county jail (if great bodily harm inflicted or prior DV conviction)
elements: Defendant committed assault, aggravated assault, battery, aggravated battery, sexual assault, stalking, kidnapping, false imprisonment, or any offense resulting in physical injury or death
The victim is a family or household member as defined in § 741.28
mandatory_minimum: 5 days county jail if great bodily harm inflicted, deadly weapon used/threatened, or prior DV conviction
enhancements: Child present during incident (mandatory BIP counseling)
Prior domestic violence conviction (mandatory 5-day jail minimum)
notes: Mandatory arrest in Florida (§ 741.2901) — officer must arrest if probable cause exists regardless of victim's wishes. No-contact order automatic upon arrest. Prosecutor can proceed without victim cooperation.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor
penalty_min: 5 days county jail (great bodily harm or prior DV conviction)
elements: Defendant actually and intentionally touched or struck the victim against the victim's will
OR Defendant intentionally caused bodily harm
Victim is a family or household member (spouse, former spouse, cohabitant, parent of common child)
mandatory_minimum: 5 days county jail minimum when great bodily harm inflicted or prior DV conviction
notes: Strangulation during domestic battery is a separate felony under § 784.041. First offense diversion programs available in some counties.

statute_title: Negligent Treatment or Maltreatment of a Child
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant is a caregiver for a child under 18
Defendant willfully or negligently failed to provide care, supervision, or services to maintain child's mental or physical health
OR Defendant failed to protect the child from abuse or exploitation
notes: § 827.03 is Florida's child abuse and neglect statute. DCF involvement is separate from criminal proceedings. Mandatory reporters who fail to report face 3rd degree felony under § 39.205.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (without great bodily harm); 1st Degree Felony (with great bodily harm)
penalty_max: 5 years (3rd); 30 years (1st degree with great bodily harm)
elements: Defendant intentionally committed an act that could reasonably be expected to result in physical or mental injury to a child
OR Defendant actively encouraged another to commit such an act
enhancements: Great bodily harm resulting (1st degree felony)
Torture or malicious punishment (aggravated child abuse — 1st degree felony)
notes: Aggravated child abuse (§ 827.03(2)(a)) — 1st degree felony includes torture, malicious punishment, or great bodily harm. Florida has mandatory minimum sentencing for sexual child abuse.

statute_title: Violation of Injunction for Protection Against Domestic Violence
offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor (first violation); 3rd Degree Felony (subsequent violation or aggravated acts)
elements: A domestic violence injunction was entered against defendant
Defendant had knowledge of the injunction
Defendant willfully violated a specific term of the injunction
enhancements: Second or subsequent violation within 5 years (3rd degree felony)
New act of violence during violation
notes: Injunction violations prosecuted separately from any new criminal charges arising from the same incident. Florida has multiple injunction types: domestic violence, sexual violence, dating violence, repeat violence, stalking.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor (basic); 3rd Degree Felony (aggravated)
elements: Defendant willfully, maliciously, and repeatedly followed, harassed, or cyberstalked the victim
The conduct caused substantial emotional distress
The conduct served no legitimate purpose
enhancements: Credible threat made (aggravated stalking — 3rd degree felony)
Violation of injunction while stalking (3rd degree felony)
notes: Cyberstalking (§ 784.048(1)(d)) includes electronic harassment across multiple platforms including doxxing and harassment campaigns.

statute_title: Abuse, Aggravated Abuse, or Neglect of an Elderly Person or Disabled Adult
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (abuse/neglect); 2nd Degree Felony (great bodily harm); 1st Degree Felony (aggravated)
elements: Victim is an elderly person (65+) or disabled adult
Defendant intentionally inflicted physical or psychological injury
OR Defendant committed an intentional act reasonably expected to result in injury
OR Defendant actively encouraged another to commit such act
enhancements: Great bodily harm resulting (2nd degree felony)
Torture or malicious punishment (aggravated — 1st degree felony)
notes: Financial exploitation of elderly (§ 825.103) prosecuted separately. Mandatory reporting requirements for caregivers. Elder financial fraud aggressively prosecuted in Florida due to large elderly population.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor (non-firearm); 3rd Degree Felony (firearm, prohibited person)
elements: Defendant knowingly carried a weapon or firearm concealed from ordinary sight
Defendant was a prohibited person OR was carrying in a prohibited location
Conduct occurred post-July 1, 2023 (permitless carry) and defendant was ineligible
enhancements: 10-20-Life if used in commission of violent crime
Convicted felon in possession (separate felony charge)
Machine gun or short-barreled weapon (2nd degree felony)
notes: Florida enacted permitless carry (Constitutional Carry) effective July 1, 2023 (HB 543). Eligible persons no longer need a permit. Remaining crimes focus on prohibited persons, prohibited places, and prohibited weapons types.

statute_title: Felons and Delinquents Possessing Firearms or Weapons
offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant has been convicted of a felony or adjudicated delinquent for a would-be felony
Defendant knowingly had in his or her care, custody, possession, or control any firearm or electric weapon
OR Defendant carried a concealed weapon
mandatory_minimum: 3 years (§ 775.087 if used in commission of another felony)
enhancements: 10-20-Life if used in commission of violent crime
Federal prosecution under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g) often concurrent
notes: Actual or constructive possession both sufficient. Restoration of civil rights does not automatically restore firearm rights in Florida.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor (basic); 2nd Degree Felony (from vehicle — drive-by)
elements: Defendant knowingly discharged a firearm
In a public place, on a highway, or over any public highway or occupied premises
In a manner or direction that exposed persons or property to risk
mandatory_minimum: 3 years minimum (§ 775.087 if in commission of a felony)
enhancements: Discharge from vehicle on public road (2nd degree felony)
notes: Drive-by shooting under § 790.19 carries separate penalties. Celebratory gunfire (New Year's) prosecuted under this statute.

statute_title: Possession of Short-Barreled Rifle, Short-Barreled Shotgun, or Machine Gun
offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant had in his or her possession, ownership, or custody a short-barreled rifle, short-barreled shotgun, or machine gun
Defendant knew the weapon was operable
enhancements: 10-20-Life if used in commission of violent crime
notes: Florida law makes possession of NFA items a 2nd degree felony even if federally registered — creating conflict with federal NFA compliance. Silencers/suppressors also regulated under § 790.222.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (under $300); 2nd Degree Felony ($300-$19,999); 1st Degree Felony ($20,000+)
elements: Defendant engaged in a scheme to defraud
Defendant obtained property by means of false or fraudulent representation
Defendant communicated via wire, radio, electromagnetic, or photooptical systems
notes: State-level communications fraud act. Federal wire fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1343) also commonly prosecuted concurrently. Pattern of activity can result in organized fraud charges under § 817.034(4).

statute_title: Criminal Use of Personal Identification Information
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (basic); 2nd Degree Felony (10-19 victims or fraud over $5,000); 1st Degree Felony (20+ victims or fraud over $50,000)
elements: Defendant willfully and without authorization fraudulently used personal identification information
The information belonged to an individual or fictitious individual
Defendant used it to obtain or attempt to obtain any benefit, compensation, credit, or access
enhancements: Using another's identity to avoid arrest
notes: Florida's identity theft statute is broad — covers use of others' information to obtain benefits of any kind. Victim counts across multiple incidents can be aggregated for enhanced charges.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (under $20,000); 2nd Degree Felony ($20,000-$99,999); 1st Degree Felony ($100,000+)
elements: Defendant was entrusted with property by another
Defendant knowingly obtained or used the property
With intent to temporarily or permanently deprive the owner
Defendant was in a position of trust or had authorized access
notes: Florida does not have a specific embezzlement statute — prosecuted as theft under § 812.014. Mandatory restitution under § 775.089.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant falsely made, altered, forged, or counterfeited a public record, certificate, deed, will, contract, note, check, or other instrument
Defendant acted with intent to injure or defraud any person
notes: Florida separates forgery (making the false instrument — § 831.01) from uttering (passing it — § 831.02). Both are 3rd degree felonies.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor (under $150); 3rd Degree Felony ($150+)
elements: Defendant drew, made, uttered, issued, or delivered a check or draft
Defendant knew at the time of issuance that there were insufficient funds
Defendant had intent to defraud
notes: Written demand providing 7 days to pay is prerequisite to prosecution under § 832.07. Diversion programs available for first offenders.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (under $20,000); 2nd Degree Felony ($20,000-$100,000); 1st Degree Felony ($100,000+)
elements: Defendant knowingly presented or caused to be presented a false or fraudulent claim for payment of a loss or injury
The claim was under any insurance policy
Defendant acted with intent to defraud
notes: Florida is a major PIP insurance fraud state. Office of Insurance Regulation and Division of Insurance Fraud actively prosecute. Organized fraud rings common.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (two or more transactions totaling $100+ within 6 months)
elements: Defendant used a credit card or account number
Defendant knew the card was stolen, forged, expired, revoked, or obtained by fraud
Defendant used it to obtain money, goods, services, or anything of value
notes: Credit card skimming devices (§ 817.625) are separately punishable as 2nd degree felony.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony ($300-$19,999); 2nd Degree Felony ($20,000-$99,999); 1st Degree Felony ($100,000+)
elements: Defendant knowingly conducted or attempted to conduct a financial transaction
The transaction involved proceeds from a specified unlawful activity
Defendant knew the property was proceeds of criminal activity
Defendant intended to promote criminal activity, avoid reporting, or conceal the nature of the proceeds
notes: Florida money laundering statute mirrors federal § 1956. Often prosecuted with drug trafficking, fraud, or organized crime. Civil forfeiture separate under Chapter 932.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (under $300); 2nd Degree Felony ($300-$19,999); 1st Degree Felony ($20,000+)
elements: Defendant engaged in a scheme to defraud
Defendant obtained or attempted to obtain property or money by means of false or fraudulent pretenses
The false representations were intentional and material
notes: Catch-all fraud statute. Florida RICO (§ 895.03) available for pattern of fraud across multiple incidents.

offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant offered or sold a security
Defendant made a false statement of material fact or omitted a material fact necessary to make the statement not misleading
Defendant acted with willful intent to defraud
enhancements: Use of interstate commerce (federal prosecution concurrent)
notes: Florida OFR and AG Economic Crimes Division prosecute. Federal SEC prosecution often concurrent. Ponzi scheme charges typically aggregated.

offense_class: Capital Felony (victim under 12, offender 18+); Life Felony (physical force, victim 12+); 1st or 2nd Degree Felony (other circumstances)
elements: Defendant committed a sexual act upon or with the victim
Defendant used force or coercion without consent
OR Victim was under 12 years of age
OR Victim was physically or mentally incapacitated
mandatory_minimum: Life without parole (victim under 12, offender 18+)
enhancements: Jimmy Ryce Act civil commitment after sentence
notes: Victim under 12 + defendant 18+ = capital felony. Mandatory sex offender registration and community notification under Chapter 943. Florida's rape shield law (§ 794.022) limits victim history evidence.

statute_title: Sexual Battery with Physical Force Likely to Cause Serious Personal Injury
offense_class: Life Felony
elements: Defendant committed a sexual act upon or with the victim
Defendant used or threatened to use a deadly weapon OR used force likely to cause serious personal injury
Without consent of the victim
mandatory_minimum: Level 9 under Criminal Punishment Code — state prison mandatory
notes: Florida does not use 'rape' in its statutes — charged as sexual battery under § 794.011. Rape shield law § 794.022 restricts victim's prior sexual history evidence.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant exposed or exhibited his or her sexual organs
The exposure occurred in a public place or in a private place exposed to public view
Defendant acted in a vulgar or indecent manner
enhancements: Victim is a minor (lewd or lascivious exhibition under § 800.04 — 2nd degree felony)
School or place where children are present
notes: If victim is under 16, charge typically elevated to lewd or lascivious exhibition (§ 800.04). Sex offender registration may be required depending on circumstances and victim age.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (first offense solicitation); 1st Degree Misdemeanor (second); 3rd Degree Felony (third+ or near school/church)
elements: Defendant solicited, induced, enticed, or procured another to commit prostitution
OR Defendant agreed to engage in prostitution for compensation
OR Defendant engaged in prostitution
enhancements: Third or subsequent offense (3rd degree felony)
Within 1,000 feet of school or church
notes: 2014 reform made purchasing sex a 3rd degree felony. John School diversion programs available. Human trafficking (§ 787.06) charged when victim is trafficked.

statute_title: Lewd or Lascivious Offenses Committed Upon or in Presence of Persons Under 16
offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony (victim 12-15); 1st Degree Felony (victim under 12)
elements: Defendant was 18 years of age or older
Defendant intentionally touched in a lewd or lascivious manner the breasts, genitals, genital area, or buttocks
Victim was under 16 years of age
mandatory_minimum: State prison presumptive for all levels
notes: Four subsections: molestation (§ 800.04(4)), conduct (§ 800.04(5)), exhibition (§ 800.04(6)), battery. Battery version — victim 12-15 is 2nd degree; under 12 is 1st degree.

statute_title: Computer Pornography and Traveling to Meet a Minor
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (solicitation); 2nd Degree Felony (traveling)
elements: Defendant knowingly used a computer or online service to solicit, lure, or entice a child under 16
Defendant believed the minor to be under 16
Solicitation was for sexual conduct
notes: Traveling to meet (§ 847.0135(4)) is a separate 2nd degree felony where actual travel occurs. FDLE conducts regular undercover operations. Federal charges commonly concurrent.

statute_title: Sexual Performance by a Child / Child Pornography
offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony (possessing); 1st Degree Felony (producing, promoting, distributing)
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed, controlled, or intentionally viewed material depicting a child under 18 engaging in sexual conduct
OR Defendant produced, promoted, financed, distributed, or possessed with intent to promote such material
mandatory_minimum: State prison presumptive
notes: Mandatory lifetime sex offender registration. FDLE actively investigates. Federal charges typically pursued concurrently.

statute_title: Sex Offender Registration — Failure to Register
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony (first offense); 2nd Degree Felony (subsequent)
elements: Defendant was a sex offender required to register under Florida law
Defendant failed to initially register, update registration, or report as required
Defendant knew or should have known of the obligation
enhancements: Failure to register and leaving the state
Second or subsequent violation (2nd degree felony)
notes: Florida has strict registration requirements — twice annual updates, report within 48 hours of address change. Cannot reside within 1,000 feet of school, park, playground, or bus stop.

statute_title: Unlawful Sexual Activity with Certain Minors
offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant is 24 years of age or older
Defendant engaged in sexual activity with a person who is 16 or 17 years of age
The minor was not the defendant's spouse at the time
enhancements: Defendant in position of authority over minor
notes: Florida's age of consent is 18. § 794.05 specifically addresses 24+ adults with 16-17 year olds. 'Romeo and Juliet' provision (§ 943.04354) allows registry removal for defendants within 4 years of victim's age.

offense_class: Capital Felony through 2nd Degree Felony (depends on circumstances)
elements: Defendant committed oral, anal, or vaginal penetration, or digital/object penetration
Without consent of victim
OR by use of force, threat, or coercion
mandatory_minimum: State prison mandatory for all felony levels
enhancements: Physical force likely to cause serious injury (life felony)
notes: Florida's primary sexual offense statute. Impaired consent through intoxication (voluntary or involuntary) is a critical issue. Florida rape shield law limits victim history evidence.

statute_title: Breach of the Peace; Disorderly Conduct
offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant engaged in an act that corrupted the public morals or outraged the sense of public decency
OR Defendant affected the peace and quiet of persons who witnessed the act
OR Defendant engaged in brawling, fighting, or tumultuous conduct
enhancements: During a state of emergency (3rd degree felony)
At a funeral or memorial service
notes: Florida's disorderly conduct requires actual public disturbance — mere offensive speech alone insufficient under First Amendment. Disorderly intoxication (§ 856.011) is a separate, lesser offense.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant resisted, obstructed, or opposed a law enforcement officer
The officer was engaged in the lawful execution of any legal duty
Defendant's resistance was without violence
notes: Resisting with violence (§ 843.01) is a 3rd degree felony. Lawfulness of the arrest is a contested defense issue in Florida courts.

statute_title: Tampering with or Fabricating Physical Evidence
offense_class: 3rd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant knew or had reasonable grounds to believe a criminal trial or proceeding was pending or would be instituted
Defendant altered, destroyed, concealed, or removed any record, document, or thing
With intent to impair its availability as evidence
notes: Witness tampering (§ 914.22) carries enhanced penalties when used to obstruct major felony prosecutions.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor (indirect contempt); Criminal contempt varies
penalty_max: 60 days or indefinite until compliance (civil contempt)
elements: A lawful court order was in effect
Defendant had knowledge of the order
Defendant willfully and intentionally disobeyed the order
enhancements: Violation of domestic violence injunction (separate criminal charge under § 741.31)
notes: Direct contempt handled summarily by the court. Indirect contempt requires show cause hearing.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant was intoxicated in a public place
AND Defendant endangered the safety of another person or property, OR caused a public disturbance
enhancements: Prior conviction within 12 months (mandatory treatment program referral)
notes: Florida requires both intoxication AND endangerment/public disturbance. Mere public intoxication alone is NOT a crime in Florida — this distinguishes it from many other states.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant loitered or prowled in a place, at a time, or in a manner not usual for law-abiding individuals
Circumstances warranted justifiable and reasonable alarm or immediate concern for the safety of persons or property
notes: Florida requires an objective reasonable officer standard. Defendant must be given opportunity to dispel alarm before arrest. Vagueness challenges frequently raised.

offense_class: 2nd Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant engaged in conduct that corrupted public morals
OR Defendant outraged the sense of public decency
OR Defendant affected the peace and quiet of persons who witnessed the act
enhancements: At school event or near place of worship
notes: Florida uses breach of peace and disorderly conduct interchangeably under § 877.03. Physical conduct required — offensive speech alone is insufficient.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor (misdemeanor underlying); 3rd Degree Felony (felony underlying)
elements: Defendant was released on bail or recognizance
Defendant was required to appear before a court for any criminal proceeding
Defendant willfully failed to appear as required
enhancements: Underlying felony charge increases FTA to felony
notes: FTA charge runs consecutive to underlying charge. Willfulness is an element — defendant must have known of the hearing. Bond forfeiture is a separate civil proceeding.

statute_title: False Reports of Commission of Crimes
offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor
elements: Defendant made a report to a law enforcement agency of a crime
The report was false
Defendant knew the report was false at the time of making it
enhancements: False report involving terrorism (3rd degree felony under § 790.163)
notes: False domestic violence allegations commonly prosecuted under this statute. Restitution to law enforcement for investigation costs available.

statute_title: Written Threats to Kill or Do Bodily Injury
offense_class: 2nd Degree Felony
elements: Defendant composed or sent any letter, inscription, or electronic record
The communication threatened to kill or do bodily injury to another person
OR Defendant made such threat via electronic communication to a school, school official, or student
notes: Unlike assault (§ 784.011), actual present ability to carry out the threat is not required. School threats receive aggressive prosecution in Florida.

offense_class: 1st Degree Misdemeanor (as component of stalking charge)
elements: Defendant engaged in a course of conduct directed at a specific person
The conduct caused substantial emotional distress
The conduct served no legitimate purpose
enhancements: Repeated course of conduct (escalates to stalking)
notes: Florida addresses harassment primarily through § 784.048 (stalking). Standalone harassment charges are typically charged within the stalking framework.

statute_title: Violation of Probation or Community Control
offense_class: Not a separate offense — defendant faces original sentencing exposure
elements: Defendant was placed on probation or community control
Defendant willfully and substantially violated a condition of probation or community control
enhancements: New law violation (substantive — typically warrants revocation)
Technical violation (failure to report, positive drug test, curfew)
notes: VOP hearings use preponderance of evidence standard. Hearsay admissible. Defendant may be held without bail pending VOP hearing.

offense_class: Not a separate class — faces original offense sentencing
elements: Defendant was on probation
Defendant violated a technical condition: failure to report, failure to pay fees, curfew violation, failed drug test, unauthorized travel, etc.
notes: Florida 2019 reform (SB 2534) — technical violations for certain non-violent offenders may result in sanctions short of revocation. Structured sanctions grid available.

statute_title: Substantive Violation of Probation (New Law Violation)
offense_class: Not a separate class — faces original sentencing plus prosecution for new offense
penalty_max: Maximum for original offense plus separate prosecution for new offense
elements: Defendant was on probation
Defendant committed a new criminal offense while on probation
enhancements: New offense is a felony (almost always results in revocation)
notes: Substantive violations almost always result in full revocation. Florida courts may impose maximum of original sentence consecutively with the new sentence.

offense_class: Not a separate class — faces original sentencing exposure
elements: Defendant was placed on community control (house arrest)
Defendant willfully and substantially violated a condition
Common violations: leaving approved residence, failure to appear for check-in, unauthorized absences
notes: Community control is a stricter alternative to probation. GPS monitoring standard. Violations treated similarly to probation violations but often result in immediate incarceration.

offense_class: Not a separate criminal offense — administrative revocation with re-imprisonment on original sentence
elements: Defendant was released on parole by the Florida Commission on Offender Review
Defendant violated one or more conditions of parole
The Florida Commission on Offender Review issued a warrant
notes: Florida abolished parole for offenses committed on or after October 1, 1983, with limited exceptions. For pre-1983 offenses, Florida Commission on Offender Review (FCOR) handles. Most modern supervision is probation or community control.

statute_title: Violation of Supervised Release / Conditional Release
offense_class: Not a separate criminal offense — administrative revocation
elements: Defendant was released on conditional release or post-prison supervisory release
Defendant violated one or more conditions of supervised release
notes: Florida's conditional release (§ 947.1405) applies to offenders serving violent felony sentences. Supervised community release under FCOR. Violations result in return to prison.

offense_class: One degree below the target offense
penalty_max: One degree below target offense maximum
fine_max: Same as one degree below target offense
elements: Defendant agreed with one or more persons to commit an offense
At least one party did an overt act in furtherance of the agreement
Defendant had specific intent to commit the target offense
enhancements: Conspiracy to commit trafficking (follows trafficking mandatory minimums under § 893.135)
notes: Florida conspiracy carries penalty one degree below completed offense, EXCEPT drug trafficking conspiracies carry same mandatory minimums as trafficking. Unlike federal law, Florida requires an overt act.

statute_title: Justifiable Use of Force / Stand Your Ground
offense_class: Affirmative defense — not a charged offense
elements: Defendant was not the initial aggressor
Defendant reasonably believed force was necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm
OR Defendant was in his or her dwelling and an intruder forcibly entered (Castle Doctrine)
Defendant had a right to be in the place where force was used (Stand Your Ground)
notes: Florida's Stand Your Ground law (§ 776.013) — no duty to retreat when in a place where defendant has a right to be. Pre-trial immunity hearing under § 776.032. After 2017 amendment, prosecution bears burden of disproving immunity by clear and convincing evidence at pre-trial hearing.

offense_class: Varies by underlying offense classification
penalty_max: Life (1st degree PBL); 30 years (1st degree felony); 15 years (2nd degree); 5 years (3rd degree); 1 year (1st degree misdemeanor); 60 days (2nd degree misdemeanor)
enhancements: Prison Releasee Reoffender (PRR) — mandatory maximum sentence
notes: Florida's Criminal Punishment Code (§ 921.002) governs felony sentencing with a scoresheet system. Prison Releasee Reoffender (PRR) requires mandatory maximum if offense committed within 3 years of release. Habitual offender designations significantly extend sentences.
